title: K-pop's top choreographer is making the AI dance version of Suno
excerpt: If you've seen a BTS or Seventeen music video, you've probably seen Choi Youngjun's work. He's trying to find a new way for dancers to make money: AI.
content_html:
Exclusive

He choreographed routines for K-pop stars like BTS and Seventeen. Now he's building AI for dance.

By Cheryl Teh

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

K-pop's biggest stars, from BTS to Seventeen, have danced routines that Youngjun Choi choreographed. Now, the top choreographer is betting that AI can help anyone with an idea, a phone, and no dance training to create the next hit K-pop dance.

It all started six years ago when Choi met Joon Jung, then a dancer in his 20s who wanted to figure out a way for choreographers to build sustainable careers.

Now, with more than 800 K-pop routines to his name, Choi has gone into business with Jung. They co-founded the startup MVNT to build an AI system for programmable dance, much like Suno, the generative AI music platform. Jung, who worked in tech and crypto, helped set up the company and is now its CEO.

In 2024, MVNT got $200,000 in seed funding from Mashup Ventures, a Seoul-based venture capital firm. Now MVNT is launching its pre-Series A fundraising and hopes to raise $1 million to take its work further.

The creative mind behind iconic K-pop dances

Choi, now in his 40s, has been in the dance business for 20 years. He's seen stars rise and fall into obscurity, and been the unseen hand behind some of the industry's most famous routines. BTS's "I Need U" — an early hit song from the Grammy-nominated group — was one of them.

The choreographer cites the band Seventeen's "Falling Flower," a complex three-and-a-half-minute routine, as one of his favorites. Choi told Business Insider dances like this can take weeks or even months to master — even for a band like Seventeen, whose members are all top-tier performers.

Despite being the creative mastermind behind K-pop stars' iconic dance moves, Choi and his peers realized they weren't creating work they could keep earning money from.

The company wasn't originally conceived as an AI startup. Instead, its goal was to solve an intellectual property problem.

"Dancers may have tens of thousands of pieces of choreography out there, but there isn't a system through which they can benefit. There's YouTube, or word of mouth. The truth is, the community isn't generating the revenue that it could," Jung told Business Insider.

Some choreographers have tried to change that. In the US, celebrity choreographer Kyle Hanagami sued Epic Games, alleging the maker of "Fortnite" copied his routines for the game. While Hanagami's case was settled, the US Copyright Office generally doesn't consider individual dance moves, short routines, or social dances to be copyrightable.

Cutting the dancers in

MVNT lets dancers build portfolios and receive credit whenever their uploaded choreography is used.

The platform then uses the choreography database to power AI tools, allowing users to input music and generate new routines.

The whole idea, the duo said, is for the dancers who create the original routines to get a piece of the profit instead of being cut out. MVNT is in the process of building its app and database — it has reached 1,100 users, and notched more than 2,000 dance routines created on the platform.

The first layer of MVNT's target audience is meme creators, much like how Suno started with casual music makers. As the model improves, Choi and Jung say the plan is to have professional choreographers use it as part of their creative process.

Enterprises, too, can use MVNT's API for animation and choreography generation.

MVNT has already shown how its tools can support animation, choreography, and interactive content creation, said Ohchan Kwon, senior evangelist at Epic Games Korea. The company worked with Epic to develop its AI-powered music-to-dance suite using Unreal Engine, Epic's 3D creation tool.

MVNT is an example of one of the companies that's driving the entertainment industry forward with their innovative work," Kwon said.

Dance should still be human-made, Choi says

Jung and Choi say people skeptical of AI-generated choreography are missing the bigger picture.

"Just like how Canva can be used to make designs, and how Suno can be used for music production, we see MVNT as a way for people to try dance and lower the barriers to entry," Jung said. "We want to make the creator ecosystem more sustainable, so dancers will be able to make enough revenue to keep doing creative work."

When asked whether AI could ever generate a routine like Seventeen member Hoshi's "Spider," — a dance Choi has called his magnum opus — Choi said MVNT isn't trying to replace choreographers.

"I think that if there were tools to help create routines now, it would open up a great deal of new possibilities for choreographers' creative directions," Choi said.

He said AI should support choreographers, rather than replace them.

"Dance is still something that comes from the heart and soul. Our intention is for the tool to be our assistant, like an employee," he said.

content_html_zh:
独家的

他为 BTS 和 Seventeen 等韩国流行歌星编排了动作。 现在他正在为舞蹈构建人工智能。

作者：Cheryl Teh 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

从 BTS 到 Seventeen，韩国流行音乐巨星都曾跳过 Youngjun Choi 编排的舞蹈。 现在，这位顶级编舞家押注人工智能可以帮助任何人只要有一个想法、一部手机，无需接受任何舞蹈训练，就能创造出下一个流行的韩国流行舞蹈。

这一切都始于六年前，当时 Choi 遇到了 Joon Jung，当时他是一名 20 多岁的舞者，他想为编舞找到一种建立可持续职业生涯的方法。

现在，Choi 已经完成了 800 多场韩国流行音乐表演，并开始与 Jung 合作。 他们共同创立了初创公司 MVNT，旨在构建可编程舞蹈的人工智能系统，就像生成式人工智能音乐平台 Suno 一样。 曾在科技和加密领域工作的荣格帮助成立了这家公司，现在是该公司的首席执行官。

2024 年，MVNT 从首尔风险投资公司 Mashup Ventures 获得了 20 万美元的种子资金。 现在 MVNT 正在启动 A 轮预筹款，希望筹集 100 万美元以进一步推进工作。

标志性韩国流行舞蹈背后的创意思维

崔现年 40 多岁，从事舞蹈事业已有 20 年。 他见证了明星的崛起和陨落，并且是一些业内最著名的惯例背后的幕后黑手。 BTS 的“I Need U”——格莱美提名乐队的一首早期热门歌曲——就是其中之一。

这位编舞家引用了十七乐队的《落花》，这是一个复杂的三分半钟的舞蹈，是他的最爱之一。 崔告诉《商业内幕》，掌握这样的舞蹈可能需要数周甚至数月的时间——即使是像“Seventeen”这样的乐队，其成员都是顶级表演者。

尽管崔和他的同事是韩国流行歌星标志性舞蹈动作背后的创意策划者，但他们意识到他们并没有创造出可以持续赚钱的作品。

该公司最初并不是被视为一家人工智能初创公司。 相反，它的目标是解决知识产权问题。

“舞者可能有数以万计的编舞作品，但没有一个系统可以让他们受益。 有YouTube，或者口碑。 事实上，社区并没有产生应有的收入，”荣格告诉《商业内幕》。

一些编舞家试图改变这一点。 在美国，名人编舞凯尔花神起诉 Epic Games，指控《堡垒之夜》的制作者抄袭了他的游戏动作。 虽然花神案已经和解，但美国版权局通常不认为个人舞蹈动作、短套路或社交舞具有版权。

将舞者切入

MVNT 允许舞者建立作品集，并在使用他们上传的编舞时获得积分。

然后，该平台使用编舞数据库来驱动人工智能工具，允许用户输入音乐并生成新的例程。

两人表示，整个想法是让创造原创动作的舞者获得一部分利润，而不是被淘汰。 MVNT 正在构建其应用程序和数据库 - 已拥有 1,100 名用户，并在该平台上创建了 2,000 多个舞蹈动作。

MVNT 的第一层目标受众是 meme 创作者，就像 Suno 最初从休闲音乐制作人开始的那样。 Choi 和 Jung 表示，随着模型的改进，他们的计划是让专业编舞者将其用作创作过程的一部分。

企业也可以使用 MVNT 的 API 来生成动画和编排。

Epic Games Korea 高级布道师 Ohchan Kwon 表示，MVNT 已经展示了其工具如何支持动画、编排和交互式内容创作。 该公司与 Epic 合作，使用 Epic 的 3D 创作工具 Unreal Engine 开发人工智能驱动的音乐舞蹈套件。

MVNT 是通过创新工作推动娱乐业向前发展的公司之一的例子，”Kwon 说。

崔说，舞蹈仍然应该是人造的

荣格和崔表示，对人工智能生成的编舞持怀疑态度的人忽视了更大的前景。

“就像 Canva 可用于进行设计，以及 Suno 可用于音乐制作一样，我们将 MVNT 视为人们尝试舞蹈并降低进入门槛的一种方式，”Jung 说。 “我们希望让创作者生态系统更加可持续，这样舞者将能够获得足够的收入来继续进行创造性工作。”

当被问及 AI 是否可以生成像 17 岁成员 Hoshi 的“蜘蛛”这样的舞蹈（Choi 称其为他的代表作）时，Choi 表示 MVNT 并不是试图取代编舞。

“我认为，如果现在有工具可以帮助创建例程，它将为编舞者的创作方向开辟大量新的可能性，”崔说。

他说人工智能应该支持编舞，而不是取代他们。

“舞蹈仍然是发自内心和灵魂的东西。 我们的目的是让该工具成为我们的助手，就像员工一样，”他说。
